about: Authored flashcard deck (memory plan 2026-09-29). Each family has a front, back, memory anchor, shape and items with a named misconception.

families.front: What does 3G do? What does G on its own do?
families.back: 3G jumps to line 3, counted from the top of the file, wherever the cursor is now. G on its own jumps to the last line of the file.
families.anchor: G = ground floor: the bottom of the file. A number in front picks the floor, counted from the top.
families.shape: {N}G = line N from the top · G alone = the last line

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 5. You type 3G. Where does the cursor go?
choices: to line 8, three lines further down
to the end of the third block of art
why: 3G always means line 3, counted from the top. Where you start does not matter.
Moving three lines down from here is 3j. G counts from the top of the file.
G counts lines, not blocks. On its own G is the last line of the whole file.
Three lines up from here is 3k. 3G is line 3 from the top.
items.misconception: 3G read as a move relative to the cursor, or as 'three blocks'

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 1. Turn the first glyph of line 3 into #.

trap_answers.why: 3j moves three lines down from line 1, so it lands on line 4. 3G goes to line 3.

items.misconception: {N}j (N lines down from here) used where {N}G (line N) was meant

families.front: Where does gg go? And where does G go?
families.back: gg goes to the first line of the file. G goes to the last line. With a number both mean that line: 4gg and 4G both go to line 4.
families.anchor: gg = the top floor; G = ground floor at the bottom.
families.shape: gg = the first line · G = the last line

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 2 of this 5-line art. Where do gg and G each take it?
choices: gg to line 1, G to line 5
gg to line 5, G to line 1
gg to line 1, G one line down to line 3
gg to the start of line 2, G to the end of line 2
why: gg is the top of the file and G is the bottom.
That swaps them. G is the ground floor, at the bottom.
G without a number never means 'one line down'; that is j.
Both jump between lines. The start and end of this row are 0 and $.
items.misconception: top and bottom swapped, or G read as a move along the row

families.front: 3j or 3G?
families.back: 3j moves three lines down from where the cursor is. 3G jumps to line 3 no matter where the cursor is.
families.anchor: j hangs down below the line, like its hook: j = down.
families.shape: {N}j = N lines down from here · {N}G = line N from the top

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 2. You type 3j, and then 3G. Which line is it on after each?
why: 3j counts from the cursor (2 + 3 = 5). 3G counts from the top.
3G does not add to where you are; it is line 3 from the top.
3j is not a line number; it moves three lines down from line 2.
The number in front of G is the line. Only G alone means the last line.
items.misconception: the number in front of G and j read the same way

families.front: What does fo do?
families.back: fo moves right along the CURRENT row to the next o. If this row has no o, nothing happens: the cursor stays. ; repeats the find on the same row.
families.anchor: f = run your finger along this row.
families.shape: f{char} = this row only · /text<CR> = the whole file

items.prompt: The cursor is at the start of line 1, which has no o. The only o is on line 2. You type fo. What happens?
choices: nothing: the cursor stays on line 1
the cursor jumps to the o on line 2
the cursor jumps to the end of line 1
an o is typed at the cursor
why: f only looks along the row the cursor is on. No o on this row, so no move.
Searching the whole file is /o then Enter. f never leaves the row.
A failed f does not move at all. The end of the row is $.
f only moves; it never types. Typing needs i, a or o first.
items.misconception: f read as a whole-file search

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 1. Change the o on line 3 into O. Line 1 has no o.

trap_answers.why: fo only searches line 1, which has no o, so the cursor stays and rO changes the | under it. Go to the row first (3G), or search the file with /o<CR>.

items.misconception: f expected to find a glyph on another row

families.front: What does /o then Enter do?
families.back: / opens a search line at the bottom of the screen. Type the text; Enter jumps to the next match anywhere in the file, even rows below. n jumps to the match after that.
families.anchor: / = search the whole file.
families.shape: /text<CR> = the next match in the file · n = the one after

items.prompt: The next o is two rows below the cursor. Which keys reach it?
why: / searches the whole file, so it can reach another row.
fo only looks along the current row.
o opens a new empty line below and starts typing.
ro replaces the cell under the cursor with o.
items.misconception: f and / treated as the same kind of search

families.front: What are the three jobs of $?
families.back: On its own, $ jumps to the end of the row (2G$ = the end of line 2). In a line range, $ is the last line (:1,3t$). At the end of a pattern, $ means 'only at the row end' (\s\+$ = spaces at the end).
families.anchor: $ = the end: the row end, the last line, or a wall the pattern must touch.
families.shape: $ = the end of the row · :1,3t$ = the last line · -$ in a pattern = only at the row end

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 4. You type 2G$. Where does it end up?
choices: on f, the last glyph of line 2
on n, two lines down at the end of the row
on the last line of the file
on c, the start of line 2
why: 2G is line 2 from the top; $ then goes to the end of that row.
2G is not 'two lines down'. Two down would be 2j.
$ on its own is the end of the ROW. The last line is G.
The start of the row would be 0 or ^. $ is the end.
items.misconception: 2G read as 'down two', or $ read as the last line

items.prompt: You run :%s/-$// on these rows. Which rows change?
choices: rows 1 and 3 lose their last -, row 2 is unchanged
every - on every row is deleted
only the first - on each row is deleted
on every row, the text from the first - to the end is deleted
why: $ is a wall: the - must touch the row end. Row 2 ends in d, so it stays.
Only a - right before the row end can match; the others stay.
The first - of a row is not at the end, so it cannot match.
$ is not 'up to the end'. The pattern is one - that touches the end.
items.misconception: pattern $ read as 'up to the end of the line'

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 1. Delete the last glyph of line 2.

trap_answers.why: 2j moves two lines down from line 1, to line 3. 2G is line 2.

items.misconception: {N}G and {N}j confused before $

families.front: What does 3yy copy? Does anything change on screen?
families.back: 3yy copies (yanks) three whole lines, starting with the cursor line. Nothing changes on screen until you put the copy somewhere with p or P.
families.anchor: yy = yank the line: the doubled letter means the whole line.
families.shape: [count] verb target: 3yy = yank 3 lines · then p puts them

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 1 of an 8-line file. What does 3yyGp do?
choices: copies lines 1-3, jumps to the last line, puts the copy below it
copies three lines and stops there
copies lines 1-3 and puts them below line 3
copies lines 1-3 and puts them at the top of the file
why: Three parts: 3yy copies, G goes to the last line, p puts below it.
That reads only 3yy. G then moves and p puts the copy.
G moved the cursor to the last line first, so p puts below line 8.
G is the bottom of the file, and p puts BELOW the cursor line.
items.misconception: 3yyGp read as only 'yank three lines'

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 1. Copy the first two lines to below the last line.

trap_answers.why: Without G the copy is put below line 1, not at the end.
P puts the copy ABOVE the cursor line, so it lands before the last line.

items.misconception: the move (G) or the direction of put (p/P) left out

families.front: After yy, where does p put the line? And P?
families.back: After copying whole lines, p puts them BELOW the cursor line and P puts them ABOVE it.
families.anchor: p = put below · P = Put above (the capital stands taller).
families.shape: p = below or after · P = above or before

items.prompt: You copied the line ab with yy. The cursor is on line 2. You type P. Where does ab appear?
choices: between 11 and 22, above the cursor line
between 22 and 33, below the cursor line
why: Capital P puts above the cursor line.
Below is lower-case p.
P uses the cursor line, not the end of the file. Go there first with G.
P adds a line; nothing is replaced.
items.misconception: p and P swapped

families.front: :s/o/O/g with nothing between : and s. Which lines change?
families.back: With nothing before s, :s changes the CURRENT line only. Put a range before s to reach more lines.
families.anchor: :s is a fill-in form: :{where}s/{find}/{replace}/{flags}.
families.shape: :{where}s/{find}/{replace}/{flags} · empty {where} = this line

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 2. You run :s/-/=/ once. What changes?
choices: only line 1, the first match in the file
why: No range before s means the current line only.
Every line needs a range: :%s/-/=/.
:s does not search the file for its first match; it works on the lines you give it.
The range is optional; without it you get the current line.
items.misconception: no range read as 'every line'

items.prompt: Change exactly the first three - into =. Leave the fourth - alone.

trap_answers.why: A number after :s counts LINES (three lines from here), not matches, so all four change.
g changes every match on the line: all four.

items.misconception: a number after :s read as a number of matches

families.front: How do you change every line? Only lines 4 to 6?
families.back: Put the lines BEFORE s. :%s/-/=/ = every line, because % means all of them. :4,6s/-/=/ = lines 4 to 6. No range = the current line.
families.anchor: % = 100% of the lines.
families.shape: :%s = every line · :4,6s = lines 4-6 · :s = this line

items.prompt: Replace every - with = on every row, with one : command.

trap_answers.why: Without g only the first - on each row changes.
No range: only the current line changes. % goes before s.

items.misconception: % placed after s, or g left out

items.prompt: Which command changes o to O on lines 4, 5 and 6 only?
why: The lines go between : and s.
Anything after the last divider is a flag or a line count, not the lines to change.
% is every line of the file.
Right after s comes the divider; the range must come before s.
items.misconception: the range written after s

families.front: What does the g at the end of :s/o/O/g change?
families.back: Without g, :s changes only the FIRST match on each line. With g it changes every match on each line. g never adds lines; the range picks the lines.
families.anchor: g flag = global on the line: every match on it.
families.shape: :s/{find}/{replace}/ = the first match per line · add g = every match

items.prompt: The cursor is on the row o-o-o. You run :s/o/O/ (no g). What is the row now?
why: Without g only the first match on the line changes.
Changing all three needs the g flag.
:s starts from the left of the row; the first match is the first o.
There is a match, so the first one changes.
items.misconception: g expected by default

families.front: What does the e in :%s/\s\+$//e do?
families.back: e keeps :s quiet when nothing matches. Without it, a search that finds nothing shows an error message. The edit itself is the same.
families.anchor: e flag = excuse the errors.
families.shape: :s/{find}/{replace}/e = no error message when nothing matches

items.prompt: No row ends in a space. What does the e change in :%s/\s\+$//e?
choices: no error message is shown; nothing is edited
it deletes to the end of every row
it edits every row even without a match
why: e only silences the 'pattern not found' error.
The pattern decides what is deleted, not e.
Rows without a match are never edited.
Asking first is the c flag.
items.misconception: e read as an edit instead of a quiet switch

families.front: In :%s/\s\+$//e, what is the job of / and of \?
families.back: / divides the parts of :s: s/find/replace/flags. \ inside the find part makes the NEXT letter special: \s = a space or tab, \+ = one or more of it. You type both keys yourself.
families.anchor: \ = a power-up for the next letter.
families.shape: s/{find}/{replace}/ · \s = space or tab · \+ = one or more

items.prompt: In :%s/\s\+$//e, what does \s mean?
choices: a space or tab: the \ makes the s special
why: \ powers up the next letter; \s matches a space or a tab.
The dividers are the / signs.
Without the \ it would be the letter s.
\ is a key you type. Escape is written <Esc>.
items.misconception: \ read as a divider or as Escape

items.prompt: In :s/o/O/g, which character separates the find part from the replace part?
why: / is the divider: s/find/replace/flags.
\ powers up the letter after it inside a pattern; it divides nothing.
$ is an end: the row end or the last line.
% before s means every line.
items.misconception: / and \ swapped

families.front: What do u and Ctrl-r do?
families.back: u undoes the last change: one step back. Ctrl-r (hold Ctrl, press r) redoes what u undid.
families.anchor: u = one step back. Ctrl-r = redo.
families.shape: u = undo one change · <C-r> = redo it

items.prompt: The row says cat. You type rX (Xat), then u (cat), then rZ (Zat). Which keys bring back Xat?
choices: none: Xat is gone for good
why: g- steps back in time across undo branches: Zat, then Xat.
u walks back along the newest branch only: Zat becomes cat.
Ctrl-r redoes an undo on this branch; after rZ there is nothing to redo.
Vim keeps both branches; g- and g+ reach them.
items.misconception: u expected to reach an older branch

items.prompt: The row was cat. Someone typed rX, u, rZ, so it says Zat. Bring back Xat.

trap_answers.why: u goes back along the newest branch, to cat. The Xat change is on the other branch: use g-.

items.misconception: the undo branch (g-) unknown

families.front: You undid a change, then made a new one. How do you get the undone version back?
families.back: u only walks back along the newest branch. The old change is on another branch. g- steps back in time across branches, g+ steps forward. :earlier 1 is the same as g-.
families.anchor: g- = a time machine across branches.
families.shape: u = back on this branch · g- / g+ = back / forward in time

items.prompt: After g- you are looking at an older version. Which key returns to the newest one?
why: g+ steps forward in time, back to the newer version.
u undoes a change; it moves further back, not forward.
gg moves the cursor to the first line; it does not touch history.
g- again goes even further back in time.
items.misconception: g+ and u confused

families.front: x or r=: which keeps the row the same width?
families.back: x deletes the cell under the cursor: the rest of the row shifts left. r{char} replaces it in place: the row keeps its width. In art, r keeps the columns lined up.
families.anchor: x = cross it out. r = replace in place.
families.shape: x = delete one cell (row shrinks) · r{char} = replace one cell

items.prompt: The row is |ab| and the cursor is on a. You type x. What is the row now?
why: x deletes the a and the rest of the row moves left.
Keeping a blank cell there is r then a space.
x is a command here, not a letter to type. Turning a into x is rx.
x deletes the cell under the cursor, not the end of the row.
items.misconception: x expected to keep the row width

items.prompt: The cursor is on the first cell. Turn the a into = without changing the row's width.

trap_answers.why: x deletes the a, so the row becomes || and loses a cell. r= replaces in place.

items.misconception: delete used where replace was meant

families.front: R==<Esc> or r=?
families.back: R types over the cells one by one until <Esc>; the row keeps its width. r{char} changes exactly one cell and returns to Normal mode by itself.
families.anchor: R = Replace until you stop.
families.shape: r{char} = one cell · R{text}<Esc> = many cells

items.prompt: The row is a--b and the cursor is on the first -. You type R==<Esc>. What is the row?
why: R overwrites two cells; the width stays the same.
Pushing text right is Insert mode (i).
That is r=: one cell only.
R only overwrites as many cells as you type.
items.misconception: R read as insert

families.front: What does o do?
families.back: o opens a NEW empty line below the cursor line and starts typing there; <Esc> ends. O opens the new line above.
families.anchor: o = open a line below.
families.shape: o{text}<Esc> = a new line below · O = above

items.prompt: The cursor is on line 1 of the rows ab and cd. You type o-<Esc>. What are the rows?
why: o opens a line right below the cursor line.
Typing at the start of the row is I.
o opens below the CURSOR line. The end of the file would be Go.
Typing at the end of the row is A.
items.misconception: o read as 'add at the end of the file'

families.front: What does :1,3t$ do?
families.back: It copies lines 1 to 3 and puts the copy below the last line. t means 'to'; here $ is the last line. :1,3t0 would put the copy at the top.
families.anchor: :t = copy lines To a place.
families.shape: :{from},{to}t{dest} = copy those lines below line {dest}

items.prompt: Copy lines 1 and 2 to below the last line with one : command.

trap_answers.why: 0 puts the copy above line 1. $ is the last line.

items.misconception: $ as a line (the last line) unknown

families.front: Does :set list change the file?
families.back: No. :set list only SHOWS hidden characters, such as spaces at the end of a row, as marks. The text is unchanged. Deleting them is still an edit: :%s/\s\+$//e or $x.
families.anchor: list = let me see the invisible.
families.shape: :set list / :set nolist = show / hide the marks · display only

items.prompt: A row ends with two spaces. You run :set list. What changed in the file?
choices: nothing: the spaces are only shown as marks
the row was cut at its last glyph
why: :set list changes the display, never the text.
Deleting them needs an edit such as :%s/\s\+$//e.
No option here turns spaces into tabs.
Nothing is cut; the marks only make the spaces visible.
items.misconception: :set list expected to clean the row

items.prompt: What does :set colorcolumn=8 do?
choices: paints screen column 8 as a ruler
lights the column the cursor is in
why: It is a painted ruler; the text is untouched.
Options like this one only change the display.
Jumping to column 8 is 8|.
That is cursorcolumn, which follows the cursor.
items.misconception: colorcolumn and cursorcolumn confused

families.front: 0 or ^: which one lands on the first glyph?
families.back: 0 jumps to column 1 of the row, even when it is a space. ^ jumps to the first glyph that is not a space.
families.anchor: 0 = column zero, the very edge. ^ = the first peak of ink.
families.shape: 0 = column 1 · ^ = the first glyph · $ = the end

items.prompt: The row is two spaces, then /\. The cursor is on the \. Where do 0 and ^ each go?
choices: 0 to the first space, ^ to the /
0 to the /, ^ to the first space
0 to the /, ^ to the end of the row
why: 0 is column 1 even when it is blank; ^ skips the spaces.
That swaps them: 0 never skips spaces.
Only ^ skips the leading spaces.
The end of the row is $.
items.misconception: 0 read as the first glyph

families.front: In 12|i|<Esc>, which | moves and which | is typed?
families.back: The first | comes after a number in Normal mode: 12| jumps to column 12. After i you are typing, so the second | is a bar glyph. With :set virtualedit=all the cursor can stand in empty columns past the row end.
families.anchor: {N}| = a fence post at column N.
families.shape: {N}| = column N · i{text}<Esc> = type before the cursor

items.prompt: In 12|i|<Esc>, what are the two | keys?
choices: the first jumps to column 12; the second is a typed bar
both are jumps to a column
the first is a typed bar; the second jumps
why: In Normal mode 12| is a move; after i every key types text.
Before i you are in Normal mode, so 12| moves the cursor.
After i, keys type text until <Esc>.
The order decides the job: move first, then type.
items.misconception: | read by its shape instead of by where it stands

items.prompt: A row has 3 cells. With virtualedit off, you type 9|. Where is the cursor?
choices: on a, because the move failed
why: Without virtualedit the cursor stops at the last real cell.
Standing in empty columns needs :set virtualedit=all first.
The move still goes as far right as the row allows.
| never changes rows.
items.misconception: empty columns expected to be reachable without virtualedit
